title: Far, Small, Sound, Sight
theme: Greek combining forms tele-, micro-, phon, scope
objectives: I can explain what tele-, micro-, phon, and scope mean.
I can use word parts to work out what a new science word means.
I can tell what each tool for seeing or sound is used for.
I can write about how an invention changed how people see, hear, or communicate.
rationale: Grade 5 moves morphology from simple affixes to Greek combining forms that carry meaning across science and history. Tele- (far), micro- (small), phon (sound), and scope (see) build ten transparent words that students can take apart and reassemble. The unit reuses the see and hear roots from grade 4 and gives students a method for new words: find the parts, predict the meaning, then check it. Most words name inventions, so the passage links word parts to the history of technology.

passage.title: Tools That Reach Far and Look Close
paras: Long ago, people could use only their own eyes and ears. Then inventors built tools that reach far away or look at tiny things. Many of their names come from Greek word parts: tele means far, micro means small, scope means to look at, and phon means sound.

In 1610, Galileo pointed a telescope at the night sky and saw four moons circling Jupiter. A microscope does the opposite kind of job. It makes tiny things look bigger. Through early microscopes in the 1600s, scientists found that a drop of pond water was full of moving creatures. Today we call such tiny living things microbes.

Other tools carry messages and sound. In 1844, a telegraph sent a message by wire from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore. In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone, which carries a voice along a wire. A microphone picks up sound, and a megaphone shapes a voice into a cone so it travels farther.

Some tools are for fun and for music. A periscope uses mirrors in a tube so a person can see over or around something, as submarine crews do. A kaleidoscope turns bits of colored glass into patterns. A symphony, played by a full orchestra, shows that sound can be art as well as information.

choices: tiny living things too small to see without a tool
qs.why: The passage says scientists found tiny moving creatures in water; microbes are tiny living things.

qs.q: Why might a periscope be useful to a submarine crew?
choices: It plays music for the crew.
It warms the water around the submarine.
It lets them see above the water while the submarine stays below.
It sends coded clicks by wire.
qs.why: The passage says a periscope lets people see over or around something, so the crew can look above the waves.

qs.q: Which detail from paragraph 3 best shows a difference between the telegraph and the telephone?
choices: The telegraph sent a message by wire, and the telephone carries a voice along a wire.
Both were invented by the same person.
qs.why: The paragraph says the telegraph sent a message while the telephone carries a voice.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Tools with Greek-based names help people see far, look closely, and share sound.
qs.why: Each paragraph gives tools whose names come from Greek parts that tell what they do.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten tool and invention words built from Greek combining forms, practice taking words apart (tele-, micro-, phon, scope), and apply a method for new words: find the parts, predict, check. They read an informational passage on the history of these tools.

notes.va.telescope.n: Anchor word for tele- and scope. Write tele + scope and ask students to predict before you define it. Do not confuse with microscope: far versus small.
notes.va.microscope.n: Pair directly with telescope on a chart: same ending scope, different first part. Students often swap them; connect micro- to small.
notes.va.microbe.n: Spelling note: micro + bio, written -be. Emphasize that most microbes are harmless or helpful; avoid equating microbe with disease.
notes.va.telegraph.n: Tele (far) + graph (write): writing sent far. Connect to the graph words in unit 8. The 1844 Washington to Baltimore line is real; use it for history links.
notes.va.telephone.n: Tele + phon + silent e. Show that phone is a clipped form. Students may know it as a verb; this unit teaches the noun.
notes.va.microphone.n: Micro + phon: small sound. Name that the word is about picking up sound, not about being small. Ask what it does with the sound.
notes.va.megaphone.n: Mega (large) + phon. Contrast with microphone: one gathers sound, the other pushes a voice outward.
notes.va.symphony.n: Sym- (together) + phon + -y. Link to grade 4's aud words: both are about sound. Play a short recording and ask which instruments join together.
notes.va.periscope.n: Peri- (around) + scope. Build a paper-tube periscope if time allows; otherwise sketch the mirror path.
notes.va.kaleidoscope.n: Origin: Greek words for beautiful and form, plus scope (the coiner was David Brewster; keep to the word parts). Show it for pattern, and relate to the shared ending -scope.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I do not know periscope. I see peri and scope. Scope looks like telescope and microscope, so it has to do with looking. Peri could be around. A tool for looking around: a tube with mirrors. I will check the definition to see if my prediction holds.'
